vo.text: Two thousand two hundred years ago, Rome sent one of the biggest armies it had ever put together into a single battle. And one man was about to teach it a lesson that soldiers still study today.
This is the Battle of Cannae.
Meet Hannibal, a general from Carthage, a city in North Africa. Two years earlier, he had marched his army over the Alps. With elephants. Just to make a point.
And meet Rome. Rome had two commanders, and they took turns being in charge. One day each. What could possibly go wrong?
On the second of August, 216 BC, the two armies met on a flat, dusty plain in southern Italy, next to a river.
Rome brought about eighty thousand soldiers. Hannibal had about fifty thousand. Rome's plan was simple. Be bigger. Push hard. Win.
Hannibal's plan was sneakier. He put his weakest troops in the middle, in a curve bulging toward the Romans. Like a bow.
His best soldiers waited at the two ends. And his horsemen guarded the sides.
The Romans charged straight at the middle. And the middle gave way. Slowly. Step by step. Exactly as planned.
The Romans thought they were winning. They pushed deeper, and deeper, into the gap.
Meanwhile, out on the sides, Hannibal's horsemen chased off the Roman cavalry. Then they swung around. Behind the Romans.
Now Hannibal's best soldiers stepped in from both ends. Left. Right. And the horsemen shut the back door.
The Roman army was completely surrounded. History's least fun group hug.
They were packed in so tightly that most of them could not even lift their swords.
By evening, Rome had lost tens of thousands of soldiers, and one of its two commanders. It was one of the worst days in Roman history.
So Hannibal won the war, right? Nope. Rome simply refused to give up. It raised new armies and kept going.
Fourteen years later, a Roman general named Scipio beat Hannibal in Africa. He had studied Hannibal's tricks very, very carefully.
Hannibal won the battle. Rome won the war. And generals have been copying his giant hug ever since.
